It’s rare and not easy for a hantavirus to spread between people. In severe cases, the virus can cause a deadly lung infection or kidney failure.As a recent deadly outbreak aboard a cruise ship in the Atlantic showed, some hantaviruses can spread between people in rare cases. The little-studied Andes hantavirus, detected in the outbreak that killed three passengers and infected several others on the MV Hondius in May, raised concerns around the world due to its mortality rate, as high as 30%, and the current lack of treatment and vaccines. Weeks later in Argentina, from where the hantavirus-stricken cruise set sail, authorities are still trying to figure out the origin of the outbreak.An early hypothesis circulated by officials suggested that patient zero, a Dutch ornithologist, may have become infected in the southernmost city of Ushuaia, famed for its location “at the end of the world." But Argentine scientists who tested rats for the Andes hantavirus in the area recently ruled out Ushuaia as the source of the outbreak — to the relief of the Antarctic cruise hub heavily reliant on foreign tourism. Argentina also concluded the wine-producing province of Mendoza was not the source of contagion earlier this month, after local investigators and biologists from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found no trace of hantavirus in rodents collected from areas visited by the Dutch man and his wife. news.content: FILE – A Venezuelan flag waves in the wind atop the National Assembly palace in Caracas, Venezuela, Jan. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Matias Delacroix, File) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: July 21, 2026 at 7:54 PM EDT | UPDATED: July 21, 2026 at 7:57 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — Venezuela confirmed on Tuesday that three people died of infections of hantavirus, but stressed there was no evidence of human-to-human transmission in the South American country, which has rarely reported cases of the rodent-borne disease in humans. The Health Ministry said hantavirus was also suspected in the deaths of two health workers in the southwestern state of Barinas. Those cases remain under investigation and were not linked to the three fatalities in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, about 655 kilometers (407 miles) away. Both states were spared the worst of the back-to-back major earthquakes that hit northern Venezuela earlier this month. The ministry described the deaths in Anzoátegui and Barinas as isolated incidents that “do not represent a risk to the general community.” But it added that health workers would be sent to the affected states to “guarantee the health security of all Venezuelans,” without elaborating. The Venezuelan Medical Federation, a national professional group, said the deaths in Anzoátegui were from the same family in the rural municipality of Miranda in the south of the state. Hantaviruses exist throughout the world and are spread mainly by contact with rodents such as rats and mice. It’s rare and not easy for a hantavirus to spread between people. In severe cases, the virus can cause a deadly lung infection or kidney failure. As a recent deadly outbreak aboard a cruise ship in the Atlantic showed, some hantaviruses can spread between people in rare cases. The little-studied Andes hantavirus , detected in the outbreak that killed three passengers and infected several others on the MV Hondius in May, raised concerns around the world due to its mortality rate, as high as 30%, and the current lack of treatment and vaccines . Weeks later in Argentina, from where the hantavirus-stricken cruise set sail, authorities are still trying to figure out the origin of the outbreak. An early hypothesis circulated by officials suggested that patient zero, a Dutch ornithologist, may have become infected in the southernmost city of Ushuaia , famed for its location “at the end of the world.” But Argentine scientists who tested rats for the Andes hantavirus in the area recently ruled out Ushuaia as the source of the outbreak — to the relief of the Antarctic cruise hub heavily reliant on foreign tourism. Argentina also concluded the wine-producing province of Mendoza was not the source of contagion earlier this month, after local investigators and biologists from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found no trace of hantavirus in rodents collected from areas visited by the Dutch man and his wife. news.content: teleSUR July 23, 2026 ES EN Opacity X X Follow us on YouTube teleSUR News Latin America World Culture Technology In Depth Sport Multimedia Galleries Infographics Opinion Articles Interviews BRICS summit Venezuela Resists ➤ Live AUDIO English Spanish Russian Chinese (Simplified) Arabic Dutch French German Portuguese Italian en ES EN Venezuelan Health Authorities Report Three Fatalities from Hantavirus The Ministry of Health specified that the event does not pose a risk to the general population and reported that the Public Health System remains deployed in the territory to safeguard health security. Photo: EFE. July 21, 2026 Hour: 4:41 pm English Spanish Russian Chinese (Simplified) Arabic Dutch French German Portuguese Italian en 🔗 Comparte este artículo PDF Venezuela’s Ministry of Health confirmed this Tuesday the deaths of 3 people in the eastern state of Anzoategui due to hantavirus infection, while stressing that the outbreak remains localized and poses no widespread risk to the general population. The Venezuelan Ministry reported on July 21, that all three victims tested positive for hantavirus after clinical and laboratory confirmation. GeographicReference The Public Health System remains deployed throughout the affected territory to monitor the situation and safeguard sanitary conditions for all Venezuelans, authorities said. RELATED: Venezuelan Acting President Rodriguez Praises Military’s Earthquake Response In a separate development, the Ministry also reported the deaths of two medical professionals in the western state of Barinas, whose causes remain under investigation. Officials were emphatic in clarifying that both events are focalized and unrelated, with no epidemiological link between the Anzoátegui outbreak and the Barinas deaths. “The definitive results of the investigation will be communicated in a timely manner through official channels,” the ministry stated. Text reads: “The Ministry of People’s Power for Health reports on recent health events reported in Anzoátegui and Barinas states. We clarify to the community that both cases respond to isolated situations that have no connection with each other and do not represent a generalized risk for the community.” Health Hantavirus is a zoonotic disease transmitted primarily by rodents in rural and agricultural environments. Humans become infected mainly by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, saliva, or droppings in enclosed spaces. According to the Ministry of Health, there is no scientific evidence of human-to-human transmission of hantavirus within Venezuelan territory. The United Nations classifies hantaviruses within the Hantaviridae family, noting they are associated with specific rodent reservoir species and can cause severe infections in humans. In the Americas, these viruses trigger hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) , a rapidly progressing respiratory and cardiac condition with a case fatality rate of up to 50 percent. Human infections typically manifest between one and eight weeks after exposure, beginning with fever, muscle aches, headaches, and gastrointestinal discomfort. The disease can evolve into HPS, characterized by cough, respiratory distress, fluid accumulation in the lungs, and shock. Because its initial symptoms mimic influenza, COVID-19, leptospirosis, and dengue, laboratory confirmation and evaluation of the patient’s history of rodent contact are essential for accurate diagnosis. The Andes virus, found in South America, remains the only hantavirus strain documented to transmit between humans, through close and sustained contact. Recent global attention to hantavirus emerged following the MV Hondius outbreak in April 2026, when an Andes virus outbreak on a cruise ship in the South Atlantic resulted in ten confirmed cases and three deaths across multiple countries, as reported by the World Health Organization. In Latin America and the Caribbean, hantavirus outbreaks are strongly influenced by environmental factors such as rainfall, temperature, and humidity, which affect rodent populations and virus transmissibility. There is currently no specific curative treatment for Hantavirus infection. Prevention relies heavily on reducing contact with rodents through environmental hygiene, proper food storage, sealing of entry points in dwellings, and avoiding the cleaning of enclosed spaces without protective equipment. Health authorities recommend ventilating closed areas for at least 30 minutes before entering, particularly in rural settings. Health System Fully Deployed The Venezuelan Ministry of Health emphasized that early medical attention is critical to improving patient survival rates. Given the similarity of initial symptoms to other febrile illnesses common in the region, health workers in Anzoátegui have been placed on alert to identify potential cases promptly and ensure rapid referral to appropriate medical facilities. Authorities urged the public to remain calm, follow official guidance, and report any suspected cases to the nearest health facility. The Ministry reiterated its commitment to transparency and public safety, stating that all updates will be communicated exclusively through official government channels. Author: Laura V. news.content_original: teleSUR July 23, 2026 ES EN Opacity X X Follow us on YouTube teleSUR News Latin America World Culture Technology In Depth Sport Multimedia Galleries Infographics Opinion Articles Interviews BRICS summit Venezuela Resists ➤ Live AUDIO English Spanish Russian Chinese (Simplified) Arabic Dutch French German Portuguese Italian en ES EN Venezuelan Health Authorities Report Three Fatalities from Hantavirus The Ministry of Health specified that the event does not pose a risk to the general population and reported that the Public Health System remains deployed in the territory to safeguard health security. Photo: EFE. July 21, 2026 Hour: 4:41 pm English Spanish Russian Chinese (Simplified) Arabic Dutch French German Portuguese Italian en 🔗 Comparte este artículo PDF Venezuela’s Ministry of Health confirmed this Tuesday the deaths of 3 people in the eastern state of Anzoategui due to hantavirus infection, while stressing that the outbreak remains localized and poses no widespread risk to the general population. The Venezuelan Ministry reported on July 21, that all three victims tested positive for hantavirus after clinical and laboratory confirmation. GeographicReference The Public Health System remains deployed throughout the affected territory to monitor the situation and safeguard sanitary conditions for all Venezuelans, authorities said. RELATED: Venezuelan Acting President Rodriguez Praises Military’s Earthquake Response In a separate development, the Ministry also reported the deaths of two medical professionals in the western state of Barinas, whose causes remain under investigation. Officials were emphatic in clarifying that both events are focalized and unrelated, with no epidemiological link between the Anzoátegui outbreak and the Barinas deaths. “The definitive results of the investigation will be communicated in a timely manner through official channels,” the ministry stated. Text reads: “The Ministry of People’s Power for Health reports on recent health events reported in Anzoátegui and Barinas states. We clarify to the community that both cases respond to isolated situations that have no connection with each other and do not represent a generalized risk for the community.” Health Hantavirus is a zoonotic disease transmitted primarily by rodents in rural and agricultural environments. Humans become infected mainly by inhaling aerosolized particles from rodent urine, saliva, or droppings in enclosed spaces. According to the Ministry of Health, there is no scientific evidence of human-to-human transmission of hantavirus within Venezuelan territory. The United Nations classifies hantaviruses within the Hantaviridae family, noting they are associated with specific rodent reservoir species and can cause severe infections in humans. In the Americas, these viruses trigger hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) , a rapidly progressing respiratory and cardiac condition with a case fatality rate of up to 50 percent. Human infections typically manifest between one and eight weeks after exposure, beginning with fever, muscle aches, headaches, and gastrointestinal discomfort. The disease can evolve into HPS, characterized by cough, respiratory distress, fluid accumulation in the lungs, and shock. Because its initial symptoms mimic influenza, COVID-19, leptospirosis, and dengue, laboratory confirmation and evaluation of the patient’s history of rodent contact are essential for accurate diagnosis. The Andes virus, found in South America, remains the only hantavirus strain documented to transmit between humans, through close and sustained contact. Recent global attention to hantavirus emerged following the MV Hondius outbreak in April 2026, when an Andes virus outbreak on a cruise ship in the South Atlantic resulted in ten confirmed cases and three deaths across multiple countries, as reported by the World Health Organization. In Latin America and the Caribbean, hantavirus outbreaks are strongly influenced by environmental factors such as rainfall, temperature, and humidity, which affect rodent populations and virus transmissibility. There is currently no specific curative treatment for Hantavirus infection. Prevention relies heavily on reducing contact with rodents through environmental hygiene, proper food storage, sealing of entry points in dwellings, and avoiding the cleaning of enclosed spaces without protective equipment. Health authorities recommend ventilating closed areas for at least 30 minutes before entering, particularly in rural settings. Health System Fully Deployed The Venezuelan Ministry of Health emphasized that early medical attention is critical to improving patient survival rates. Given the similarity of initial symptoms to other febrile illnesses common in the region, health workers in Anzoátegui have been placed on alert to identify potential cases promptly and ensure rapid referral to appropriate medical facilities. Authorities urged the public to remain calm, follow official guidance, and report any suspected cases to the nearest health facility. The Ministry reiterated its commitment to transparency and public safety, stating that all updates will be communicated exclusively through official government channels. Author: Laura V. "There is no scientific evidence of person-to-person transmission in our country."Anzoategui, located roughly 300 kilometers (186 miles) east of the capital Caracas, is a largely rural, agricultural state where health officials say rodent exposure is more common. Barinas sits in Venezuela's western plains region, near the border with Colombia.Following the confirmed diagnoses, authorities established an epidemiological containment zone in Anzoategui to identify potential contacts and intensify public health surveillance. Boats approach the Dutch flagged hantavirus-stricken cruise ship MV Hondius after it arrived at the industrial port of Granadilla de Abona on the island of Tenerife in Spain's Canary Islands on May 10, 2026. (AFP Photo) Rare person-to-person spreadHantaviruses are a family of viruses spread mainly by rodents that can cause severe, sometimes fatal, respiratory and hemorrhagic conditions in humans. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates between 10,000 and 100,000 human cases occur globally each year, with severity depending on the specific viral strain.Human-to-human transmission remains extraordinarily rare worldwide, though the Andes virus strain is the only known hantavirus variant capable of spreading through close, prolonged contact between people. US passengers from the Dutch flagged hantavirus-stricken cruise ship MV Hondius disembark at the industrial port of Granadilla de Abona on the island of Tenerife in Spain's Canary Islands on May 10, 2026. (AFP Photo) 'Rapidly spreading threat'The Venezuelan Medical Federation expressed concern Monday, urging the national government to act swiftly against what it described as a rapidly spreading threat.The federation disputed the government's account, asserting that the epidemiological situation is more severe than official figures suggest. According to the medical association, patients across affected areas are presenting with a high fever, internal bleeding and acute respiratory failure. The group criticized the health ministry's lack of transparency, calling for comprehensive investigations and open public communication. Hantavirus Alert in Venezuela: 3 Dead, 2 Suspected Casesfollow usfollow usVenezuela has confirmed three deaths linked to hantavirus infections, while health authorities are investigating two additional suspected deaths involving healthcare workers in the southwestern state of Barinas. Although the developments have raised concerns, officials have emphasized that there is no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission in the country and that the reported cases remain isolated. The confirmed fatalities occurred in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, while the two suspected cases under investigation were reported in Barinas, nearly 655 kilometers away. According to the Venezuelan Health Ministry, there is currently no epidemiological link between the two clusters, and the incidents do not pose an immediate risk to the general public. Breaking It DownWhat is the Andes strain of hantavirus?How does the Andes strain differ from other hantaviruses?What are the symptoms of Andes hantavirus infection?Created with AI.Health teams have nevertheless been deployed to the affected regions to strengthen surveillance and containment efforts.Also read: World Brain Day: One Silent Health Condition Could Raise Your Stroke Risk DramaticallyWhat is Hantavirus? Hantavirus is a group of viruses primarily spread by infected rodents, particularly rats and mice. Humans typically become infected after inhaling virus-containing particles released through rodent urine, droppings, or saliva. Less commonly, infection can occur through rodent bites or by touching contaminated surfaces and then touching the face. The disease is relatively rare but can be extremely serious. Depending on the virus strain, hantavirus infection can lead to: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS): A severe lung disease that can rapidly progress to respiratory failure. Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS): A condition that primarily affects the kidneys and can lead to kidney failure. Signs and symptoms of Hantavirus infection Early symptoms often resemble those of the flu, making diagnosis challenging. Common warning signs include: Fever and chills Severe muscle aches Fatigue Headache Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain As the illness progresses, patients may develop a persistent cough, breathlessness, chest tightness, difficulty breathing, and low blood pressure. Doctors say these symptoms require immediate medical attention, as severe cases can become life-threatening within days.Can Hantavirus spread between people? In most cases, hantavirus does not spread from person to person. The majority of infections worldwide occur through contact with infected rodents or their contaminated environments. However, certain strains - particularly the Andes hantavirus found in South America - have demonstrated rare instances of human-to-human transmission. Earlier this year, a deadly outbreak aboard the Antarctic-bound cruise ship MV Hondius highlighted these concerns after several passengers became infected. Even so, experts stress that such transmission remains uncommon and is limited to specific virus strains.Why are the Venezuela cases important? Hantavirus infections are rarely reported in Venezuela, making the recent deaths noteworthy for public health authorities. The Venezuelan Medical Federation reported that the three confirmed victims in Anzoátegui belonged to the same family living in a rural municipality, suggesting a shared environmental exposure rather than community transmission. Meanwhile, scientists in Argentina continue investigating the source of the recent Andes hantavirus outbreak. Studies have already ruled out several suspected locations after extensive rodent testing, underscoring how difficult it can be to identify the exact origin of these infections.Ways to prevent Hantavirus infection Since rodents are the primary source of infection, prevention focuses on reducing exposure: Keep homes and food storage areas free of rodents. Seal holes and cracks that allow rodents to enter buildings. Wear gloves and a mask when cleaning rodent-infested areas. Avoid sweeping dry rodent droppings; disinfect the area first. Store food in sealed containers and dispose of garbage properly. news.source_body_en: Venezuela is grappling with a hantavirus outbreak, confirmed to have claimed three lives in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, with two additional suspected cases involving healthcare workers in the southwestern state of Barinas. Health authorities have stressed that these cases remain isolated, with no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission or community spread. The incidents, separated by approximately 655 kilometers, show no epidemiological link, and officials assure the public of no immediate risk. Health teams have been deployed to enhance surveillance and containment efforts. The outbreak is notable as hantavirus infections are rarely reported in Venezuela, with the confirmed cases linked to a family in a rural municipality, suggesting environmental exposure rather than person-to-person spread.

All you need to know as three dead in VenezuelaMost hantaviruses do not spread between humans, although person-to-person transmission is possibleCopy linkBookmarkCommentsGo to commentsBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarksClose popoverPowered By 10 Sec 10.1K 00Spanish health ministry provides update on cruise ship hit by hantavirusNext video inShareNextKEEP WATCHINGRelated: Spanish health ministry provides update on cruise ship hit by hantavirusThree people have died in Venezuela from hantavirus infections, authorities confirmed on Tuesday, stressing there was no evidence of human-to-human transmission in the country.Hantavirus was also suspected in the deaths of two health workers in the southwestern state of Barinas, the Health Ministry said, however these cases remain under investigation and were not linked to the three fatalities in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, some 655 kilometres away.The deaths in Anzoátegui and Barinas were described by the ministry as isolated incidents that "do not represent a risk to the general community." Nevertheless, it said health workers will be sent to the affected states to "guarantee the health security of all Venezuelans," without elaborating.A national professional group, The Venezuelan Medical Federation, said the deaths in Anzoátegui were from the same family in the rural municipality of Miranda in the south of the state.RECOMMENDEDNearly half of Americans think Trump’s DC projects are just to feed his egoBear who climbed telephone pole in viral video has diedDermatologists Reveal Link between Aging and Pillowcases Blissy | SponsoredSponsoredStudy Shows Surprising Link Between Aging & your PillowcaseBlissy | SponsoredSponsoredopen image in galleryThree people died after being exposed to a rare hantavirus strain while on the MV Hondius cruise (Getty)It comes after three people died and 13 were infected after being exposed to a rare hantavirus strain, the Andes virus, while on the MV Hondius cruise. What is hantavirus?Hantavirus is mainly spread by contact with rodents or their urine, saliva or droppings, particularly when the material is disturbed and becomes airborne, posing a risk of inhalation.People are typically exposed to hantavirus around their homes, cabins or sheds, especially when cleaning out enclosed spaces with little ventilation or going into areas where there are mouse droppings.Hantavirus is “such a severe disease” there are global efforts to try and develop vaccines against it, according to Professor Robin May, chief scientific officer at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The virus is widespread around the world.“The Andean strain, is the only one for which there is some evidence in the past of human-to-human transmission,” he told BBC Breakfast.The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began tracking the virus after a 1993 outbreak in the Four Corners region – the area where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet.It was a doctor with the Indian Health Service who first noticed a pattern of deaths among young patients, said Michelle Harkins, a pulmonologist with the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center who for years has been studying the disease and helping patients.open image in galleryThe US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began tracking the virus after a 1993 outbreak (Reuters)Most US cases are in Western states. New Mexico and Arizona are hotspots, Dr Harkins said, likely because the odds are greater for mouse-human encounters in rural areas.Symptoms of hantavirusAn infection can rapidly progress and become life-threatening. Experts say it can start with symptoms that can include:Fever Chills Muscle aches Headache “Early in the illness, you really may not be able to tell the difference between hantavirus and having the flu,” said Dr Sonja Bartolome of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.Symptoms of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome usually show between one and eight weeks after contact with an infected rodent. As the infection progresses, patients might experience tightness in the chest as the lungs fill with fluid.open image in galleryHantavirus is mainly spread by contact with rodents or their urine, saliva or droppings (AFP/Getty)The other syndrome caused by hantavirus — haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome — usually develops within a week or two after exposure.Death rates vary depending on which hantavirus causes the illness. Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is fatal in nearly 40 per cent of people infected, while the death rate for haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome varies from 1 per cent to 15 per cent of patients, according to the CDC.How to prevent hantavirusThere is no specific treatment or cure, but early medical attention can increase the chance of survival.Despite years of research, Dr Harkins said many questions have yet to be answered, including why the illness can cause mild symptoms for some people and very severe symptoms for others. She and other researchers have been following patients over long periods of time in hopes of finding a treatment.“A lot of mysteries,” she said, noting that what researchers do know is that rodent exposure is a key.open image in galleryHealth officials previously assured the public that there was no risk of a global outbreak following the MV Hondius cruise passengers’ disembarkation (AFP/Getty)The best way to avoid infection is to minimise contact with rodents and their droppings, and use protective gloves and a bleach solution for cleaning up rodent droppings.Public health experts caution against sweeping or vacuuming, which can cause the virus to get into the air.How is hantavirus different from Covid?Unlike Covid, most hantaviruses do not spread between humans, although person-to-person transmission is possible.RECOMMENDEDBurnham says Whitehall’s days of resisting devolution are ‘over’Fox News host and father of daughters says educated women become ‘ugly’ and ‘bitter’Which Fee-Only Financial Advisor Firms Ranked Highest in 2026?SmartAsset | SponsoredSponsoredAsk a Pro: "Will a Financial Advisor Outperform My Self-Directed Brokerage?"SmartAsset | SponsoredSponsoredHealth officials previously assured the public that there was no risk of a global outbreak following the MV Hondius cruise passengers’ disembarkation.The chief of the WHO, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “This is not another Covid. news.content: AZ EN Region World AnewZ Originals AI & Next Business Culture Green Programmes Investigations Opinion Live Live Region World AnewZ Originals AI & Next Business Culture Green Programmes Investigations Opinion AnewZ Talks Follow Us Home Health Health news Hantavirus Venezuela Venezuela confirms three hantavirus deaths, says no sign of person-to-person spread A test tube labelled "Hantavirus positive" is held in this illustration taken 7 May 2026 Reuters By Chigozie Ohaka , Agencies July 22, 2026 04:55 Copied Venezuelan health authorities have confirmed that three people have died from hantavirus infections, while stressing there is no evidence that the disease is spreading between people in the country. The deaths occurred in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, an area where human cases of the rodent-borne virus are rarely reported. Officials described the cases as isolated incidents and said there was currently no threat to the wider population. At the same time, health officials are investigating the deaths of two healthcare workers in the southwestern state of Barinas, where hantavirus is also suspected. Authorities said those cases remain under review and are not connected to the fatalities reported in Anzoátegui, which lies roughly 655 kilometres away. According to the Venezuelan Medical Federation, the three victims in Anzoátegui belonged to the same family and lived in the rural municipality of Miranda. The Health Ministry said medical teams would be deployed to the affected areas to strengthen surveillance and ensure public health protections, although it did not provide further details about the response. Hantaviruses are found in many parts of the world and are most commonly transmitted through contact with infected rodents such as rats and mice. Human infections are generally rare, and transmission from one person to another is considered uncommon. In severe cases, the virus can lead to serious respiratory illness or kidney failure. EU pledges €20 million more for Venezuela after deadly earthquakes Hantavirus cruise ship arrives in Rotterdam, crew quarantined and disinfected The announcement comes amid heightened international attention on hantavirus following a deadly outbreak aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius earlier this year. That outbreak, linked to the Andes strain of hantavirus, killed three passengers and infected several others, raising concerns because some variants of the virus can occasionally spread between humans. Scientists are still investigating the origins of that cruise ship outbreak. Researchers in Argentina have already ruled out several early theories, including suggestions that the virus may have originated in Ushuaia, known as the world's southernmost city, or in the wine-producing province of Mendoza. While health authorities continue to monitor developments, Venezuelan officials maintain that the recent deaths do not indicate a broader outbreak and that there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission within the country. Scientists are still investigating the origins of that cruise ship outbreak. Researchers in Argentina have already ruled out several early theories, including suggestions that the virus may have originated in Ushuaia, known as the world's southernmost city, or in the wine-producing province of Mendoza. While health authorities continue to monitor developments, Venezuelan officials maintain that the recent deaths do not indicate a broader outbreak and that there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission within the country. news.content: Venezuela confirms three hantavirus deaths, rules out human-to-human transmission Venezuela’s Health Ministry has confirmed three deaths linked to hantavirus in the northeastern state of Anzoategui, while stating that there is currently no evidence of person-to-person transmission of the virus in the country, Qazinform News Agency cites Xinhua. "We report the regrettable deaths of three patients in Anzoategui with confirmed diagnoses of hantavirus," the ministry said in a statement. The ministry added that there was "no scientific evidence of person-to-person transmission in our country," explaining that hantavirus is primarily spread through contact with rodents, particularly in rural and agricultural areas. Health authorities also clarified that the confirmed hantavirus cases were not connected to the recent deaths of two healthcare workers in the southwestern state of Barinas. The causes of those deaths remain under investigation. The ministry said the final results of ongoing investigations would be announced once they are available. Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that the European Union had received an emergency shipment of an experimental antiviral drug that may be used to treat Hantavirus infections

(PHOTO / AP) CARACAS – Venezuela's Health Ministry on Tuesday confirmed three deaths from hantavirus in the northeastern state of Anzoategui, while ruling out evidence of person-to-person transmission in the country."We report the regrettable deaths of three patients in Anzoategui with confirmed diagnoses of hantavirus," the ministry said in a statement. It added that there was "no scientific evidence of person-to-person transmission in our country," noting that the virus is transmitted by rodents in rural and agricultural areas.READ MORE: Venezuela quake death toll rises to 4,490The ministry also said the cases were unrelated to two recent deaths of healthcare workers in the southwestern state of Barinas, whose causes have yet to be confirmed.Authorities said the final results of the investigations would be released in due course. analysis.brief_en: Venezuela's Health Ministry has confirmed three hantavirus-related deaths in the northeastern state of Anzoategui, explicitly ruling out person-to-person transmission. The ministry stated the virus is transmitted by rodents in rural and agricultural areas, emphasizing no scientific evidence of human-to-human spread exists locally. The outbreak highlights ongoing risks in rodent-prone regions while reinforcing current transmission understanding.

analysis.time: Published on 2026-07-21. Event date: Tuesday (announcement date for Venezuela cases); cruise ship outbreak occurred between April 1 and May (final inspection on May 29).
analysis.location_and_population: Venezuela: eastern Anzoategui state (3 deaths) and Barinas state (2 unlinked deaths). Cruise ship MV Hondius: departed Argentina for Cape Verde on April 1.
analysis.event: Confirmed hantavirus outbreak in Venezuela's Anzoategui state with 3 deaths; 2 additional unlinked deaths in Barinas state under investigation. Separately, a cruise ship outbreak (MV Hondius) linked to Andes virus resulted in 3 deaths and 13 infections.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Venezuela: 3 confirmed deaths in Anzoategui, 2 unlinked deaths in Barinas. Cruise ship: 3 deaths, 13 infections. Venezuelan health ministry states no community risk and no evidence of person-to-person transmission.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Venezuelan health ministry announced cases and emphasized no community risk. Cruise ship outbreak: Dutch public health service declared no public health obstacles to ship operation after final inspection on May 29. No new cruise ship cases reported since May. Barinas deaths remain under investigation.

analysis.brief_en: Venezuela's health ministry reported three confirmed hantavirus deaths in Anzoategui state, sparking outbreak concerns, while two additional unlinked deaths in Barinas state remain under investigation. Separately, a cruise ship outbreak linked to the Andes virus resulted in three deaths and 13 infections. Venezuelan authorities emphasized no community risk and no evidence of person-to-person transmission. The Dutch public health service cleared the MV Hondius for operation after declaring no public health obstacles following a final inspection on May 29, with no new cases reported since then. The incidents highlight ongoing hantavirus risks in both community and travel settings.

Enjoy FDA: Our Cyclospora Finding Was a False Positive NYC Legionnaires' Outbreak Has Now Taken 3 Lives Malaria Vaccine's Achilles' Heel: Its 4th Dose Second Death Reported in NYC Legionnaires' Outbreak Health | hantavirus US Passengers Describe Their Days in Hantavirus Quarantine Americans were held in Nebraska for prolonged confinement that some call a civil liberties violation By Polly Davis Doig withNewser.AI Posted Jul 22, 2026 9:59 AM CDT Copied Nebraska Medicine's Davis Global Center is seen on Sunday, May 10, 2026, in Omaha, Neb., where American passengers from the hantavirus-stricken cruise ship MV Hondius will quarantine. (AP Photo/Rebecca S. Gratz) See 1 more photo They signed up for a rare and expensive birding cruise; they say they ended up in a de facto jail run by the US government. Eighteen Americans evacuated from the MV Hondius amid a deadly Andes hantavirus outbreak were flown to a federal quarantine unit in Omaha on May 11, and told to expect a brief evaluation before finishing isolation at home, reports the New York Times. None tested positive. Days later, a CDC doctor informed them they'd be held at least two more weeks—and, for some, ultimately as long as 42 days—under orders signed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has campaigned against strict COVID-era measures. Passengers describe harshly lit rooms, limited outdoor access, bungled meals, and growing psychological strain; one man threatened suicide when New York initially refused to accept his return home under CDC conditions. "This is a civil liberties violation," he tells the Times. Some echoed the sentiment and likened the facility to a "prison," especially after Kennedy overruled CDC medical advice to keep Florida resident Angela Perryman in Omaha instead of allowing monitored home quarantine. After a trickle of releases, the final eight passengers were allowed to leave on June 21, notes the AP. Federal officials say the strict approach worked: the US recorded no hantavirus cases or community spread. Read These Next Courtney Stodden is calling Jason Alexander out over a 2012 sketch. (AP Photo/Rebecca S. Gratz) See 1 more photo They signed up for a rare and expensive birding cruise; they say they ended up in a de facto jail run by the US government. Eighteen Americans evacuated from the MV Hondius amid a deadly Andes hantavirus outbreak were flown to a federal quarantine unit in Omaha on May 11, and told to expect a brief evaluation before finishing isolation at home, reports the New York Times. None tested positive. Days later, a CDC doctor informed them they'd be held at least two more weeks—and, for some, ultimately as long as 42 days—under orders signed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has campaigned against strict COVID-era measures. Passengers describe harshly lit rooms, limited outdoor access, bungled meals, and growing psychological strain; one man threatened suicide when New York initially refused to accept his return home under CDC conditions. "This is a civil liberties violation," he tells the Times. Some echoed the sentiment and likened the facility to a "prison," especially after Kennedy overruled CDC medical advice to keep Florida resident Angela Perryman in Omaha instead of allowing monitored home quarantine. After a trickle of releases, the final eight passengers were allowed to leave on June 21, notes the AP. news.content_title: Man in Lviv region found to have hantavirus after vacation in Croatia and trip to mountains
news.content: Man in Lviv region found to have hantavirus after vacation in Croatia and trip to mountains July 23, 2026 at 10:03 AM • 2646 переглядiв A resident of Stryi was diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by hantavirus. The man recently returned from a vacation in Croatia and traveled through the Ivano-Frankivsk region. In the Lviv region, a case of hantavirus infection has been confirmed in a 53-year-old man; the specific location and circumstances of infection have not yet been established, reported the Lviv Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention on July 23, writes UNN . In the Lviv region, a case of hantavirus infection has been laboratory confirmed. A 53-year-old resident of the city of Stryi has been confirmed to have hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by hantavirus The disease, as stated, began on July 12 with a rise in body temperature to 38.6 °C, chills, headache, nausea, loss of appetite, and pain in the calf muscles. On July 15, the man sought medical attention at the Lviv Regional Infectious Diseases Clinical Hospital, where he was hospitalized with a preliminary diagnosis of "unspecified bacterial infection". The study of biological material was conducted by the laboratory of particularly dangerous infections of the State Institution "Lviv Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine". According to the results of laboratory tests: no antibodies to Leptospira interrogans (leptospirosis) were detected in the blood serum; no DNA of Leptospira interrogans (leptospirosis) was detected in the urine; RNA of hantavirus was detected in the blood serum by PCR method As noted, "during the epidemiological investigation, it was established that from July 1 to July 7, the man was on vacation in Croatia, on the Makarska Riviera, where he swam in the Adriatic Sea. He traveled in his own car." "On July 11, the man traveled through the mountainous areas of the Ivano-Frankivsk region. On his way home, he stopped in the village of Kamianka, Stryi district, where he washed his hands in the Kamianka River," the report states. At the same time, as reported, "the patient denies contact with mouse-like rodents, their nests or excretions, being in basements, as well as consuming food or water that could have been contaminated with rodent excretions." Currently, the specific location and circumstances of infection have not been established. Swimming in the sea and washing hands in the river are mentioned as part of the epidemiological history, but are not a confirmed route of infection At the patient's place of residence, as stated, anti-epidemic and preventive measures are being carried out. The epidemiological investigation is ongoing. news.content: In Ukraine uk ru en Home News Publications Blogs Contacts Legislation In Ukraine In the World Society Sud Info Judicial Practice Auto Sports SUD info SUD info In Ukraine In Lviv region, a man was diagnosed with hantavirus after traveling abroad 19:08, 23 July 2026 280 The illness began with a body temperature rise to 38.6 °C, chills, headache, nausea, loss of appetite, and calf muscle pain. Follow the latest news on SUD.UA social networks In the Lviv region, a case of hantavirus infection was laboratory confirmed. A 53-year-old resident of the city of Stryi was diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by hantavirus. Only the latest: read SUD.UA on Telegram According to the Lviv Regional Center for Disease Control and Prevention of the Ministry of Health of Ukraine, the first symptoms appeared on July 12. The man’s temperature rose to 38.6 °C, accompanied by chills, headache, nausea, loss of appetite, and calf muscle pain.Дізнатися більшеЗаконодавствоСхідноєвропейцігазету On July 15, the patient sought medical help at the Lviv Regional Infectious Clinical Hospital, where he was hospitalized with a preliminary diagnosis of "unspecified bacterial infection." During laboratory examination, no signs of leptospirosis were found in his blood and urine. At the same time, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of his blood serum confirmed the presence of hantavirus RNA. During the epidemiological investigation, it was established that from July 1 to 7, the man vacationed in Croatia on the Makarska Riviera, and on July 11, he traveled through the mountainous areas of the Ivano-Frankivsk region. On his way home, he stopped in the village of Kamianka in the Stryi district, where he washed his hands in a river. At the same time, the patient denies contact with rodent-like mice, their nests or secretions, as well as being in basements or consuming potentially contaminated food or water. Experts emphasize that the exact place and circumstances of infection have not yet been established. Staying in Croatia and washing hands in the river are only part of the epidemiological history and do not confirm the route of infection. Anti-epidemic and preventive measures are being carried out at the patient’s place of residence. The epidemiological investigation is ongoing. According to medical professionals, hantaviruses are mainly carried by rodent-like mice. Humans most often become infected by inhaling dust contaminated with their secretions or through contact with contaminated food, water, or surfaces.Дізнатися більшеВерховний судПравова допомогаЮридичні новини Initial symptoms of the infection may resemble leptospirosis or other acute infectious diseases. The main manifestations include high fever, severe weakness, headache, muscle pain, nausea, and loss of appetite. In severe cases, kidney dysfunction, reduced urine output, swelling, and a sharp drop in blood pressure may occur. As previously reported by the "Judicial and Legal Newspaper", cases of hantavirus infection, transmitted by rodents, have already been recorded in Ukraine. Medical professionals stress that after contact with mice, their secretions, or being in premises with signs of rodents, it is necessary to immediately consult a doctor, as the disease can rapidly progress and cause severe lung damage. Doctors advise to always inform medical personnel about possible contact with rodents or being in places where signs of mice were noticed. Such information will help to suspect hantavirus infection more quickly and prescribe the necessary examinations. Experts warn against self-medication or waiting for symptoms to pass on their own. Before seeing a doctor, it is recommended to limit physical activity, as lung involvement may worsen the condition. Also, it is advised not to return to dusty premises where rodents may have been to avoid repeated contact with potentially contaminated dust. analysis.time: Publication date: 2026-07-23. Event date: Symptoms began on July 12, 2026; patient sought medical help on July 15, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Region: Lviv region, specifically the city of Stryi. Affected population: A 53-year-old man.
analysis.event: A 53-year-old man from Stryi, Lviv region, was diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by hantavirus after traveling abroad. The diagnosis was laboratory confirmed via PCR testing of blood serum. The exact place and circumstances of infection have not been established.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases: 1 confirmed case. Deaths: Not reported. Exposures: The patient vacationed in Croatia (Makarska Riviera) from July 1-7 and traveled through mountainous areas of Ivano-Frankivsk region on July 11. Risk: Not explicitly stated in the evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Response: The patient was hospitalized at Lviv Regional Infectious Clinical Hospital. Anti-epidemic measures are being carried out at his place of residence. Uncertainty: The exact place and route of infection remain under investigation; the patient denied contact with rodents or their secretions.

analysis.brief_en: A 53-year-old man in Ukraine's Lviv region has been diagnosed with hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome caused by hantavirus, marking a confirmed case following laboratory testing. The patient, a resident of Stryi, first exhibited symptoms on July 12, including high fever, chills, headache, nausea, and muscle pain, and sought medical care on July 15. Epidemiological investigation revealed he had traveled to Croatia's Makarska Riviera (July 1-7) and passed through mountainous areas of Ivano-Frankivsk region (July 11), though the exact infection source remains undetermined. Health authorities emphasize that while rodent exposure is the primary transmission route, this case highlights the importance of vigilance for travelers and prompt medical consultation. The ongoing investigation underscores the challenges in pinpointing hantavirus exposure sites, particularly when patients report no direct rodent contact.

The patient, a resident of Stryi, first exhibited symptoms on July 12, including high fever, chills, headache, nausea, and muscle pain, and sought medical care on July 15. supplementary_news.content: Three people have died in Venezuela from hantavirus infections, authorities confirmed on Tuesday, stressing there was no evidence of human-to-human transmission in the country. Hantavirus was also suspected in the deaths of two health workers in the southwestern state of Barinas, the Health Ministry said, however these cases remain under investigation and were not linked to the three fatalities in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, some 655 kilometres away. The deaths in Anzoátegui and Barinas were described by the ministry as isolated incidents that "do not represent a risk to the general community." Nevertheless, it said health workers will be sent to the affected states to "guarantee the health security of all Venezuelans," without elaborating. A national professional group, The Venezuelan Medical Federation, said the deaths in Anzoátegui were from the same family in the rural municipality of Miranda in the south of the state. Three people died after being exposed to a rare hantavirus strain while on the MV Hondius cruise (Getty) It comes after three people died and 13 were infected after being exposed to a rare hantavirus strain, the Andes virus, while on the MV Hondius cruise. What is hantavirus? Hantavirus is mainly spread by contact with rodents or their urine, saliva or droppings, particularly when the material is disturbed and becomes airborne, posing a risk of inhalation. People are typically exposed to hantavirus around their homes, cabins or sheds, especially when cleaning out enclosed spaces with little ventilation or going into areas where there are mouse droppings. Hantavirus is "such a severe disease" there are global efforts to try and develop vaccines against it, according to Professor Robin May, chief scientific officer at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA). The virus is widespread around the world. "The Andean strain, is the only one for which there is some evidence in the past of human-to-human transmission," he told BBC Breakfast . The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began tracking the virus after a 1993 outbreak in the Four Corners region – the area where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet. It was a doctor with the Indian Health Service who first noticed a pattern of deaths among young patients, said Michelle Harkins, a pulmonologist with the University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center who for years has been studying the disease and helping patients. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began tracking the virus after a 1993 outbreak (Reuters) Most US cases are in Western states. New Mexico and Arizona are hotspots, Dr Harkins said, likely because the odds are greater for mouse-human encounters in rural areas. Symptoms of hantavirus An infection can rapidly progress and become life-threatening. Experts say it can start with symptoms that can include: "Early in the illness, you really may not be able to tell the difference between hantavirus and having the flu," said Dr Sonja Bartolome of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas. Symptoms of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome usually show between one and eight weeks after contact with an infected rodent. As the infection progresses, patients might experience tightness in the chest as the lungs fill with fluid. Hantavirus is mainly spread by contact with rodents or their urine, saliva or droppings (AFP/Getty) The other syndrome caused by hantavirus — haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome — usually develops within a week or two after exposure. Death rates vary depending on which hantavirus causes the illness. Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome is fatal in nearly 40 per cent of people infected, while the death rate for haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome varies from 1 per cent to 15 per cent of patients, according to the CDC. How to prevent hantavirus There is no specific treatment or cure, but early medical attention can increase the chance of survival. Despite years of research, Dr Harkins said many questions have yet to be answered, including why the illness can cause mild symptoms for some people and very severe symptoms for others. She and other researchers have been following patients over long periods of time in hopes of finding a treatment. "A lot of mysteries," she said, noting that what researchers do know is that rodent exposure is a key. Health officials previously assured the public that there was no risk of a global outbreak following the MV Hondius cruise passengers' disembarkation (AFP/Getty) The best way to avoid infection is to minimise contact with rodents and their droppings, and use protective gloves and a bleach solution for cleaning up rodent droppings. Public health experts caution against sweeping or vacuuming, which can cause the virus to get into the air. How is hantavirus different from Covid? Unlike Covid, most hantaviruses do not spread between humans, although person-to-person transmission is possible. Health officials previously assured the public that there was no risk of a global outbreak following the MV Hondius cruise passengers' disembarkation. The chief of the WHO, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: "This is not another Covid. The current public health risk from hantavirus remains low. My colleagues and I have said this unequivocally, and I will say it again to you now."

supplementary_news.content: FILE – A Venezuelan flag waves in the wind atop the National Assembly palace in Caracas, Venezuela, Jan. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Matias Delacroix, File) By Associated Press PUBLISHED: July 21, 2026 at 4:54 PM PDT | UPDATED: July 21, 2026 at 4:57 PM PDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — Venezuela confirmed on Tuesday that three people died of infections of hantavirus, but stressed there was no evidence of human-to-human transmission in the South American country, which has rarely reported cases of the rodent-borne disease in humans. The Health Ministry said hantavirus was also suspected in the deaths of two health workers in the southwestern state of Barinas. Those cases remain under investigation and were not linked to the three fatalities in the eastern state of Anzoátegui, about 655 kilometers (407 miles) away. Both states were spared the worst of the back-to-back major earthquakes that hit northern Venezuela earlier this month. The ministry described the deaths in Anzoátegui and Barinas as isolated incidents that “do not represent a risk to the general community.” But it added that health workers would be sent to the affected states to “guarantee the health security of all Venezuelans,” without elaborating. The Venezuelan Medical Federation, a national professional group, said the deaths in Anzoátegui were from the same family in the rural municipality of Miranda in the south of the state. Hantaviruses exist throughout the world and are spread mainly by contact with rodents such as rats and mice. It’s rare and not easy for a hantavirus to spread between people. In severe cases, the virus can cause a deadly lung infection or kidney failure. As a recent deadly outbreak aboard a cruise ship in the Atlantic showed, some hantaviruses can spread between people in rare cases. The little-studied Andes hantavirus , detected in the outbreak that killed three passengers and infected several others on the MV Hondius in May, raised concerns around the world due to its mortality rate, as high as 30%, and the current lack of treatment and vaccines . Weeks later in Argentina, from where the hantavirus-stricken cruise set sail, authorities are still trying to figure out the origin of the outbreak. An early hypothesis circulated by officials suggested that patient zero, a Dutch ornithologist, may have become infected in the southernmost city of Ushuaia , famed for its location “at the end of the world.” But Argentine scientists who tested rats for the Andes hantavirus in the area recently ruled out Ushuaia as the source of the outbreak — to the relief of the Antarctic cruise hub heavily reliant on foreign tourism. Argentina also concluded the wine-producing province of Mendoza was not the source of contagion earlier this month, after local investigators and biologists from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention found no trace of hantavirus in rodents collected from areas visited by the Dutch man and his wife.
